extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, journalists, and policymakers interested in public opinion, propaganda, and political psychology
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze how stereotypes, codes, and myths structure perception and public opinion, and use practical clues (contradictions, space, time, motive-attribution) to detect and critique those stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception is a mix of reality and expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: The way we see things is a combination of what is there and of what we expected to find.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that observers will 'visualize with the aid of images already in our mind' (e.g., mistaking a stranger for a friend from a hat and gait). When evaluating claims or reports, account for the role of prior expectations in shaping perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertness widens aspects and discounts expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Expertness in any subject is a multiplication of the number of aspects we are prepared to discover, plus the habit of discounting our expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts perceive more individuating detail and (ideally) correct for stereotypes; novices tend to compress variety into familiar types. Use domain expertise to expand discriminations and lower reliance on stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes standardize and then distort description
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypes constructed as simplified diagrams become popularized and supply standard versions of social roles, leading observers to read those qualities back into real people and events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be suspicious of 'official portraiture' or simplified models (e.g., economic caricatures of capitalist/worker/consumer) that fit outcomes and then are taken as the cause; check whether the model's assumed actors and world actually match the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirmation bias of entrenched stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: When a system of stereotypes is well fixed, attention is called to facts which support it, and diverted from those which contradict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate which facts are being highlighted vs. ignored. Look for selection of supportive statistics, anecdotes, and 'inside truth' used to reinforce rival narratives; require evidence that addresses disconfirming data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral codes presuppose factual maps
rubrics_metrics.description: At the core of every moral code there is a picture of human nature, a map of the universe, and a version of history; rules apply only insofar as those factual assumptions hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging an action by a code, make explicit the underlying factual assumptions (psychology, institutions, history). If those assumptions differ between interlocutors, critiques should address those factual disagreements rather than only the moral formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference in factual assumptions outweighs difference in ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: Far more serious than any difference of moral code is the difference in the assumptions about facts to which the code is applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In debates, reexamine 'visions of the facts' rather than only comparing competing ideals or maxims. Probe participants' background factual suppositions (e.g., human nature uniformity vs. variability) as the root of disagreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myth lacks critical separation of truth and error
rubrics_metrics.description: A myth may contain much true material but never contains the critical power to separate its truths from its errors; it treats opinion as unquestionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply tests of evidence even to widely accepted narratives. Treat even plausible myths as hypotheses requiring proof and open to contradiction; avoid accepting mythic explanations simply because they cohere emotionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect false absolutism via internal contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Contradictory principles used together (each blanketing different objections) reveal that argumentation has been constructed to obliterate inconvenient facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for cases where multiple, mutually exclusive principles are invoked in sequence to justify different claims (example: annexing territory alternately on geographic, historic, racial, reparations, cultural, and defense grounds). Use contradiction as a red flag of manufactured absolutism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect stereotype by failure to account for space
rubrics_metrics.description: An inability to take account of space (logistical/geographical realities) is a clue to a stereotype dominating thought rather than practical appraisal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether advocates ignore distances, transport, or practical geography (e.g., invoking an 'Eastern Front' supplied by Japan to reach Germany despite 5,000 miles of intervening territory). Require attention to actual means of movement and logistics, not just abstract maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceive space practically, not geometrically
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical life understands space in terms of available transportation and routes, not as geometric straight lines; maps must be read with transport, speed, and routes in mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating territorial or operational plans, include constraints: what ships/roads/rails exist, their speed, capacity, costs, and detours. Avoid reasoning from 'as the crow flies' distances without operational context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect stereotype by misuse of time scales
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to use the appropriate time-conception (e.g., treating transient institutions as permanent) leads to error; wise judgment distinguishes which time-conception applies to a decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure decisions and evaluations match the relevant time horizon (immediate emergency vs. long-term policy). Watch for attempts to fossilize short-term arrangements into permanent rules (e.g., overly rigid wills or unamendable constitutions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal perspective depends on discriminations in experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Vividness of time (the 'ideational present') is proportionate to the number of discriminations perceived within it; different creatures or people may 'feel' time differently, affecting judgments about duration and change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for subjective differences in perceived duration when interpreting testimony, memory, or public reaction. Recognize that fast-moving or intensely discriminated periods feel long in memory but short in experience, and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opponents may be seeing different facts, not acting in bad faith
rubrics_metrics.description: When two factions each see vividly their own aspect, they seldom credit the other with honesty; they mistake different perception for perversity or malign intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before imputing bad faith, test whether disagreement arises from differing perceptual patterns or underlying stereotypes. Seek to reveal and compare the factual maps each side uses rather than assuming deliberate deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency to villainize and posit conspiracies
rubrics_metrics.description: Out of opposition people make villains and conspiracies—labeling profiteers, agitators, foreign plots for diverse social problems; the search for plots can explain many phenomena but often overreaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of conspiracy explanations that homogenize diverse events under a single grand plot. Demand specific causal evidence for alleged conspiracies and consider simpler explanations (mismanagement, market forces, structural factors) before adopting conspiratorial narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codes produce role-dependent assumptions about human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Different codes (patriotic, economic, professional) assume different human motives—e.g., patriotic codes assume self-sacrifice, economic codes assume incentive-driven behavior—so the same person can be interpreted differently under different codes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit which code is being applied when evaluating behavior. Avoid one-code explanations for complex behavior; consider that actors may display different motives in different social roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of codes requires interpreters and contextualization
rubrics_metrics.description: Around every code there is a cloud of interpreters who deduce more specific cases; applying a general rule to a concrete situation involves interpretive judgment and potential ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When instructing or judging behavior by codes (legal, moral, professional), specify interpretive principles and criteria for borderline cases (e.g., self-defense definitions, provocation). Recognize that disputes about application often hinge on interpretation rather than disagreement about the rule itself.
